strengths: The coordinate-only virtual-correspondence construction is an original and useful approach to approximate pose estimation. Reusing established five-point and P3P solvers makes the difficult 4p3v problem accessible, especially through the simple, training-free mean-point variant.

The central empirical result has substantial support: 10,000 real image triplets, controlled noise experiments, and synthetic-only training of the learned predictor. In Table 1, the learned solver improves AUC@10 over homotopy continuation from 50.80 to 54.35 on Sacre Coeur and from 31.74 to 33.95 on St. Peters’ Square. The mean-point solver achieves approximately comparable performance to the much more complicated homotopy method.

Including the strong 5pt+P3P baseline provides useful practical guidance. The paper candidly acknowledges that this baseline generally performs better and that virtual correspondences introduce errors even without measurement noise. These comparative findings contribute value independently of benchmark leadership.

The supplementary experiment on 9,900 image pairs provides concrete evidence that the idea transfers to two-view estimation. The supplement also describes the network architecture, geometric loss, synthetic-data generation, and major training settings. Together, the methodological simplicity and supported empirical findings favor weak acceptance.
weaknesses: The evaluation leaves an important component of three-camera geometry untested. Section 5 measures rotations and unit translation directions for pairs 1–2 and 1–3. These metrics, and the corresponding Sampson residuals, cannot detect an incorrect relative translation scale between the two baselines. No relative-scale or joint three-view reconstruction error is reported.

The demonstrated efficiency advantage is limited. In Table 1, the learned solver takes 38.50 and 14.13 seconds per triplet, versus 2.59 and 2.46 seconds for 5pt+P3P, which generally also achieves better accuracy. The mean variant primarily offers implementation simplicity. Controlled outlier-rate experiments or comparisons at equal runtime are absent, so the proposed practical advantage of smaller samples remains unverified.

The approximation's operating range is insufficiently characterized. Figure 2 establishes favorable average behavior, but does not reveal failure tails or sensitivity to perspective distortion, triangle extent, and scene depth. Figures 3–4 show appreciable translation error even on noiseless inputs. The two-scene real benchmark does not establish robustness across these geometric conditions.

Reproduction of the experimental comparisons is hindered by missing GC-RANSAC thresholds, stopping settings, local-optimization details, and rules for selecting among multiple five-point/P3P solutions in the noise experiment. These choices affect both accuracy and runtime. The promised implementation release cannot substitute for information available in the submitted manuscript.

A secondary issue concerns the interpretation of the oracle experiments: they are informative references, but are not established precision upper bounds under noisy inputs. Supplying one exact correspondence does not guarantee a bound on pose error when the remaining correspondences are noisy.
